---
title: "Quiz: crowded spots and evaluation"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Spots are Gaussians of width σ; the "gate" is the largest distance at which a detection may be matched to a true spot.

---

**Q1.** Two equal spots of σ = 2 px are 5 px apart. Do they give two maxima in the raw image? After a matched filter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$2\sigma$ raw, $2\sqrt2\,\sigma$ after the matched filter.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Raw: $2\sigma = 4 < 5$: two maxima (with a shallow dip). After the matched filter the width is $2\sqrt2 = 2.83$, and $2 \times 2.83 = 5.66 > 5$: one maximum. The detector sees one candidate.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why is there a trade-off between false spots and merged spots in the choice of the filter width?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Recall [unit 2](../spot-threshold/lec.qmd): how does the number of noise maxima depend on σ_f?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A wider filter smooths the noise more: fewer noise maxima (their number scales with $1/\sigma_f^2$), so fewer false spots at a given threshold. But it also widens the spots, $\sigma_\text{eff}^2 = \sigma^2 + \sigma_f^2$, so neighbours merge at larger distances. The matched filter (σ_f = σ) is the usual compromise.
:::

---

**Q3.** Fitting two spots instead of one always gives a smaller residual. Why is that not enough reason to keep two?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What can a second spot fit when there is only one?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A model with more parameters can always fit the data at least as well: with one real spot, the second spot fits a bit of noise and lowers the residual a little. Keep two spots only if the improvement exceeds a penalty for the extra parameters (e.g. $3c\sigma_n^2$ with $c$ = 2 or ln(#pixels)); otherwise single spots get phantom partners.
:::

---

**Q4.** What are TP, FP and FN when evaluating a spot detector, and why must the matching be one-to-one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two detections near one true spot.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
TP: a detection matched to a true spot within the gate; FP: a detection not matched; FN: a true spot not matched. One-to-one: otherwise two detections on one spot would both count as TP (and one detection between two spots would count twice), inflating precision and recall.
:::

---

**Q5.** Give an example where greedy matching (closest pair first) gives fewer matches than the optimal matching.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two truths, two detections on a line.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Truths at 0 and 2.5, detections at 1 and −2, gate 2.5. Greedy takes 1–0 (distance 1) first; then the detection at −2 is 4.5 from the truth at 2.5: one match. Optimal: 1–2.5 (1.5) and −2–0 (2.0): two matches.
:::

---

**Q6.** You report F1 = 0.95 with a gate of 5 px for spots of σ = 1.5 px. What is suspicious?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What can be matched at 5 px?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A gate of 5 px (more than 3σ) accepts detections that are far off, and in dense images it can match a detection to a neighbouring spot. The F1 then hides poor localisation. Use a gate of about σ to 2σ, report the RMSE of the matched pairs too, and show F1 against the gate: a good detector has a flat F1 well below 5 px.
:::

---

**Q7.** A detector is systematically 0.5 px off to the right (a bug in the pixel-centre convention). Which numbers in the evaluation show it, and which do not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Detection vs localisation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With a gate of 2 px, F1 hardly changes: the detections are still within the gate. The RMSE grows (0.5 px in quadrature with the random error), and the **mean offset** (the average of detection − truth) shows it directly as about (+0.5, 0). Always report the mean offset as well as the RMSE.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the sum of two equal Gaussians of width σ at $\pm d/2$ has a single maximum at the centre if and only if $d \le 2\sigma$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compute the second derivative at the centre.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$f(x) = g(x - d/2) + g(x + d/2)$, $g(x) = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$, $g''(x) = (x^2/\sigma^4 - 1/\sigma^2)g(x)$. Then $f''(0) = 2g''(d/2) = \frac{2}{\sigma^2}\big(\frac{d^2}{4\sigma^2} - 1\big)g(d/2)$, negative (a maximum at the centre) iff $d < 2\sigma$. For $d < 2\sigma$ one can also check that $f' < 0$ for all $x > 0$, so the centre is the only maximum; for $d > 2\sigma$ the centre is a local minimum between two maxima.
:::
